notes.definition: Halide ions in solution are identified by adding dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution. They form precipitates of silver halides: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide a cream precipitate and iodide a yellow precipitate.
explanation: Halide ions are the negative ions of the Group 7 elements: chloride (Cl⁻), bromide (Br⁻) and iodide (I⁻). To test a solution for halide ions, first add a few drops of dilute nitric acid, then add a few drops of silver nitrate solution. If a halide ion is present, a precipitate of the silver halide forms. The colour of the precipitate tells you which halide ion is present.

Chloride ions give a white precipitate of silver chloride (AgCl). Bromide ions give a cream precipitate of silver bromide (AgBr). Iodide ions give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI). Because the colours are similar shades, it helps to compare the precipitate with known samples, and to look against a dark background.

The nitric acid is added first to remove any carbonate ions. Carbonate ions would also react with silver ions to form a precipitate, which could be mistaken for a silver halide. The acid reacts with carbonate to form carbon dioxide, so it is removed. Hydrochloric acid must NOT be used, because it contains chloride ions, which would give a white precipitate of silver chloride whatever the sample contained. Nitric acid is used because silver nitrate already contains nitrate ions, so nothing new is added that could form a precipitate.

The precipitates form because silver halides are insoluble in water. For example: NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) and KI(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgI(s) + KNO₃(aq). In the ionic equation (Higher tier) only the silver and halide ions take part: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). The sodium or potassium ions and the nitrate ions are spectator ions. The halide test is part of required practical 7.
keyFacts: Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution.
Chloride (Cl⁻): white precipitate of silver chloride, AgCl.
Bromide (Br⁻): cream precipitate of silver bromide, AgBr.
Iodide (I⁻): yellow precipitate of silver iodide, AgI.
Nitric acid removes carbonate ions, which would also form a precipitate.
Do not use hydrochloric acid: it adds chloride ions.

keyTerms.definition: A negative ion of a Group 7 element, such as Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻.
AgNO₃, a soluble silver compound used to test for halide ions.
An insoluble compound of silver with a halide ion, such as AgCl, AgBr or AgI.
To add acid to a solution, here to remove carbonate ions before the test.
An ion that is present but does not take part in the reaction.

equations.name: Silver chloride precipitate

equations.name: Ionic equation (HT)
equations.formula: silver ion + halide ion → silver halide

workedExamples.title: Identifying a halide
workedExamples.question: Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of a potassium salt. A cream precipitate forms. Name the salt.
steps: A cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows bromide ions.
The salt is a potassium salt, so it contains K⁺.
K⁺ and Br⁻ combine as KBr.

workedExamples.title: Writing equations
workedExamples.question: Write the full and ionic equations for the reaction of sodium iodide solution with silver nitrate solution.
steps: Swap partners: sodium iodide + silver nitrate → silver iodide + sodium nitrate.
NaI(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgI(s) + NaNO₃(aq). It is already balanced.
Remove spectator ions Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ for the ionic equation.
workedExamples.answer: NaI(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgI(s) + NaNO₃(aq); Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s)

workedExamples.title: Choosing the right acid
workedExamples.question: A student acidifies a solution with dilute hydrochloric acid before adding silver nitrate, and gets a white precipitate. Can she conclude the solution contained chloride ions?
steps: These chloride ions react with silver nitrate to give white silver chloride, whatever was in the sample.
So the white precipitate may come from the acid, not the sample.
workedExamples.answer: No; the test is invalid. She should repeat it using dilute nitric acid.

diagrams.title: Why nitric acid is used
diagrams.caption: Nitric acid removes carbonate ions (which would give a precipitate) without adding chloride ions. Hydrochloric acid would add Cl⁻ and give a false white precipitate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often acidify with hydrochloric acid because it is the most common acid.
misconceptions.right: In fact hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions, which give a white precipitate with silver nitrate. Dilute nitric acid must be used.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the acid is added to make the precipitate form.
misconceptions.right: In fact the acid removes carbonate ions, which would otherwise form a precipitate and give a false result.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up bromide and iodide colours.
misconceptions.right: In fact bromide gives cream and iodide gives yellow; chloride gives white.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write the precipitate as 'silver nitrate'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the precipitate is the silver halide, such as silver chloride (AgCl); silver nitrate is the soluble reagent.

realWorld: Water companies test drinking water for chloride ions using silver nitrate-based methods.
Silver halides are light-sensitive and were used in traditional photographic film.
Food chemists use silver nitrate titrations to measure the salt (sodium chloride) content of foods.
higherTier: Ionic equations: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s); Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s); Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s).
separateOnlyContent: The test for halide ions with acidified silver nitrate (part of required practical 7) is in separate Chemistry only (8462).
examTips: State the reagents in order: 'add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution'.
Colours: chloride white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. Learn them in Group 7 order: they get darker down the group.
If asked why nitric acid and not hydrochloric acid, give both points: to remove carbonate ions, and HCl would add chloride ions.
Name the precipitate as the silver halide, for example 'silver bromide'.
summary: Test: dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution.
Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow precipitate.
Acid removes carbonate; do not use HCl.

questions.question: Which reagents are used to test for halide ions?
options: Dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride
Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate
markScheme: 1 mark: Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate
questions.explanation: Halides are tested with acidified silver nitrate. Barium chloride tests for sulfate; NaOH for metal ions; limewater for CO₂.

questions.question: What colour precipitate forms when chloride ions react with acidified silver nitrate?
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is white. Bromide gives cream and iodide gives yellow.

questions.question: Which ion gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate?
questions.explanation: Silver iodide is yellow.

questions.question: What colour is silver bromide?
questions.explanation: Silver bromide is a cream precipitate.

questions.question: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate?
options: To make the precipitate a brighter colour
questions.explanation: Carbonate ions would also form a precipitate with silver ions, so they are removed as CO₂ first.

questions.question: Why must hydrochloric acid NOT be used to acidify the sample in the halide test?
options: It reacts with silver nitrate to give a white precipitate whatever the sample
markScheme: 1 mark: It reacts with silver nitrate to give a white precipitate whatever the sample
questions.explanation: HCl contains Cl⁻ ions, which always give white AgCl with silver nitrate.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a student adding potassium iodide solution to acidified silver nitrate solution.
A precipitate forms.
What is the precipitate?
questions.explanation: Silver ions combine with iodide ions to form insoluble silver iodide. Potassium nitrate stays in solution.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate when sodium bromide reacts with silver nitrate?
questions.explanation: Silver ions are Ag⁺; one Ag⁺ combines with one Br⁻. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.

questions.question:
A student tested a solution.
The student did not add acid before adding silver nitrate.
Table 1 shows the results.
What was in the solution?
questions.explanation: Silver carbonate reacts with acid (fizzing, CO₂) and dissolves; silver halides do not dissolve in nitric acid. This shows why acid is added first.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of tests on solution X.
What is solution X?
questions.explanation: Yellow flame: sodium. Cream precipitate: bromide.

rows: Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution

questions.question: Describe how to test a solution for halide ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: then add silver nitrate solution (and look for a precipitate)
questions.explanation: Both reagents in the correct order are needed.

questions.question: Give the colour of the precipitate formed with acidified silver nitrate by: (a) chloride ions, (b) bromide ions, (c) iodide ions.
questions.explanation: The colours are required knowledge for this test.

questions.question: Explain why dilute nitric acid, rather than dilute hydrochloric acid, is used in the halide test.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions
1 mark: which would form a white precipitate (silver chloride) with silver nitrate, giving a false positive
questions.explanation: Nitric acid removes carbonate without adding any ion that would form a precipitate.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction between sodium chloride solution and silver nitrate solution, with state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct state symbols, with (s) for AgCl
questions.explanation: The silver chloride is the solid precipitate; sodium nitrate stays dissolved.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction that forms a yellow precipitate in the halide test.
questions.explanation: Yellow is silver iodide. Only the silver and iodide ions react.

questions.question: A student finds it hard to decide whether a precipitate is white or cream. Suggest two ways she could make the result more certain.
markScheme: 1 mark: compare it with precipitates from known chloride and bromide solutions
1 mark: view the tubes against a dark background / side by side
questions.explanation: The colours are similar shades, so side-by-side comparison with references is good practice.

questions.question:
A student tested a white solid.
Table 1 shows the results.
Name the solid and write its formula.
questions.explanation: Lilac flame shows K⁺; white precipitate shows Cl⁻.

rows: Dissolve in water, add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution

questions.question: Name the precipitate formed when chloride ions react with silver nitrate.
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is an insoluble white solid.

questions.question: A technician has three solutions: sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide. Describe how the technician could identify each solution using chemical tests.
markScheme: Indicative content: put a small sample of each into separate test tubes
Add a few drops of dilute nitric acid to each
Add a few drops of silver nitrate solution
Compare side by side / against a dark background
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct reagents in order and all three colours linked to the correct ions
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): silver nitrate mentioned with one or two correct colours
questions.explanation: All three are sodium salts, so only the halide test distinguishes them.

questions.question: A student is told that a solution may contain carbonate ions and one type of halide ion. Describe and explain how the student could find out whether carbonate ions are present and which halide ion is present. Include an ionic equation for each precipitate or gas you describe.
markScheme: Indicative content: add dilute nitric acid to a sample
Fizzing shows carbonate; gas turns limewater milky (CO₂)
Continue adding nitric acid until fizzing stops so all carbonate is removed
Explain: carbonate would otherwise form a precipitate with silver ions
Explain why HCl is not used (adds chloride ions)
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): logical sequence with correct reagents, explanations and correct ionic equations
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): carbonate and halide tests described with some explanation or equations
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one test described
questions.explanation: The best answers use the acid step both as the carbonate test and as the preparation for the halide test, with ionic equations.

questions.question: Which of these would give NO precipitate with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution?
questions.explanation: Sodium nitrate contains no halide ions. The other three contain Cl⁻, I⁻ and Br⁻.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of silver nitrate?
questions.explanation: Silver is Ag and the nitrate ion is NO₃⁻; silver ions are Ag⁺, so the formula is AgNO₃.

questions.question: Explain why a precipitate forms when silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing bromide ions.
acceptedAnswers: silver ions combine with bromide ions
markScheme: 1 mark: silver ions combine with bromide ions
1 mark: silver bromide is insoluble in water, so it forms a solid precipitate
questions.explanation: Precipitates form when ions from two solutions combine to make an insoluble compound.

questions.question:

What can the student conclude?
options: Nothing about halides in the sample, because HCl supplied chloride ions
markScheme: 1 mark: Nothing about halides in the sample, because HCl supplied chloride ions
questions.explanation: The chloride ions from the acid cause the white precipitate, so the test is invalid.

rows: 1. Add dilute hydrochloric acid to the sample

questions.question:
A student tested a solution.
Table 1 shows the results.
Name the compound in the solution and give its formula.
questions.explanation: Green hydroxide shows Fe²⁺; white silver halide shows Cl⁻. Fe²⁺ needs two Cl⁻.

rows: Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution

questions.question: Tap water is tested with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution. A faint white cloudiness appears. What does this suggest?
options: The water contains a small amount of chloride ions
markScheme: 1 mark: The water contains a small amount of chloride ions
questions.explanation: A white precipitate shows chloride ions; faint cloudiness means a low concentration. Carbonate is removed by the nitric acid, and iodide would be yellow.
